questions.q: The rms value of an alternating current of peak value $I_{0}$ is:
questions.solution:
$I_{\text{rms}} = \mathbf{\dfrac{I_{0}}{\sqrt2}} \approx 0.707\,I_{0}$.

The rms value is the steady current that would produce the same heat — which is why the mains is quoted as $220$ V although it peaks at about $311$ V.

questions.q: The reactance of a capacitor in an AC circuit:
questions.solution:
$X_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$, so it **falls** as frequency rises.

At high frequency the capacitor barely has time to charge before the voltage reverses, so it hardly opposes the current at all — and at DC ($\omega = 0$) it blocks completely.

questions.q: The average power consumed over a full cycle by a pure inductor carrying alternating current is:
questions.solution:
In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by exactly $90°$, so the power factor $\cos\phi = \cos 90° = 0$ and the average power is **zero**.

Energy flows into the magnetic field for a quarter cycle and back out the next — it is borrowed, never spent. Such a current is called **wattless**.

questions.q: At resonance in a series LCR circuit:
questions.solution:
At resonance $\mathbf{X_{L} = X_{C}}$, so they cancel, the impedance drops to its minimum $Z = R$, and the current is at its greatest.

$\omega_{0} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. This is exactly how a radio is tuned: the set is made to resonate at one station's frequency.

questions.q: A step-up transformer increases the voltage. It therefore:
questions.solution:
An ideal transformer conserves power: $V_{p}I_{p} = V_{s}I_{s}$.

Raising the voltage must therefore **lower** the current in the same proportion.

That is precisely why power is transmitted at high voltage: the line loss $I^{2}R$ falls as the square of the current.

questions.q: The rms voltage of the mains is $220$ V. Find its peak value, in volts, correct to the nearest volt.
questions.solution:
$V_{0} = \sqrt2\,V_{\text{rms}} = 1.414 \times 220 \approx \mathbf{311}$ V.

Insulation has to withstand the **peak**, not the rms — which is why the difference matters in practice.

questions.q: Find the reactance (in ohms) of a $0.5$ H inductor at $50$ Hz. Take $\pi = 3.14$.
A series circuit has $R = 3\,\Omega$, $X_{L} = 8\,\Omega$ and $X_{C} = 4\,\Omega$. Find the impedance, in ohms.
questions.solution:
$Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + \left(X_{L} - X_{C}\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \mathbf{5}\,\Omega$.

The reactances are subtracted first because they act in opposite directions — and only then combined with $R$ at right angles.

questions.q: Find the resonant frequency (in Hz) of a series circuit with $L = 2$ H and $C = 32\,\mu$F. Take $\pi = 3.14$.
A transformer has $100$ turns in the primary and $500$ in the secondary. If the primary voltage is $220$ V, find the secondary voltage, in volts.
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} \Rightarrow V_{s} = 220 \times \dfrac{500}{100} = \mathbf{1100}$ V.

A step-up transformer, and the current in the secondary will be a fifth of that in the primary.

questions.q: For a series LCR circuit, derive the expression for the impedance and the phase angle between voltage and current.
questions.solution:
The same current $I$ flows through all three, so take it as the reference.

**The three voltages.**

$V_{R} = IR$ — in phase with the current.

$V_{L} = IX_{L}$ — leads the current by $90°$.

$V_{C} = IX_{C}$ — lags the current by $90°$.

$V_{L}$ and $V_{C}$ are exactly opposite, so they partly cancel, leaving $\left|V_{L} - V_{C}\right|$ at right angles to $V_{R}$.

**Adding by Pythagoras:**

$V = \sqrt{V_{R}^{2} + \left(V_{L} - V_{C}\right)^{2}} = I\sqrt{R^{2} + \left(X_{L} - X_{C}\right)^{2}}$.

$\mathbf{Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + \left(X_{L} - X_{C}\right)^{2}}}$ and $\mathbf{\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_{L} - X_{C}}{R}}$.

If $X_{L} > X_{C}$ the circuit is inductive and the current lags; if $X_{C} > X_{L}$ it leads.

questions.q: Explain the working of a transformer, write the turns relation, and give two sources of energy loss with their remedies.
questions.solution:
**Working.** Two coils are wound on a common soft-iron core. Alternating current in the primary makes an alternating flux in the core; that flux links the secondary and induces an emf in it.

A transformer therefore works on **AC only** — with DC the flux would be steady and nothing would be induced.

**Turns relation** (ideal): $\dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} = \dfrac{I_{p}}{I_{s}}$.

**Losses and remedies.**

1. **Copper loss** — $I^{2}R$ heating in the windings. Remedy: thick, low-resistance wire.

2. **Eddy current loss** — currents induced in the core. Remedy: laminate the core.

3. **Hysteresis loss** — energy spent re-magnetising the core each cycle. Remedy: a soft magnetic material with a narrow hysteresis loop, such as silicon steel.

4. **Flux leakage** — not all the flux reaches the secondary. Remedy: wind the coils one over the other on a closed core.

questions.q: A series LCR circuit has $R = 10\,\Omega$, $L = 0.1$ H and $C = 100\,\mu$F, across a $220$ V AC supply. Find the resonant angular frequency, the impedance at resonance, the current, and the power factor.
questions.solution:
**Resonant angular frequency.**

$LC = 0.1 \times 100 \times 10^{-6} = 10^{-5}$, so $\sqrt{LC} = 3.16 \times 10^{-3}$.

$\omega_{0} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{3.16 \times 10^{-3}} \approx \mathbf{316}$ rad/s (about $50$ Hz).

**Impedance at resonance.** $X_{L}$ and $X_{C}$ cancel exactly, so $Z = R = \mathbf{10\,\Omega}$ — the smallest it ever gets.

**Current.** $I = \dfrac{V}{Z} = \dfrac{220}{10} = \mathbf{22}$ A, the largest it ever gets.

**Power factor.** $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = 1$ — the circuit behaves as if it were purely resistive.

At resonance the inductor and capacitor pass energy back and forth between them, and the supply is left doing nothing but replacing what the resistor turns into heat.

questions.q: Define power factor and explain why a low power factor is undesirable in power transmission.
questions.solution:
**Definition.** $\cos\phi$, where $\phi$ is the phase angle between voltage and current; equivalently $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z}$.

The average power is $P = V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi$, so only that fraction of the apparent power does any work.

**Why a low power factor is bad.** To deliver a given real power $P$ at a low $\cos\phi$, the current must be larger:

$I = \dfrac{P}{V\cos\phi}$.

A larger current means larger $I^{2}R$ losses in the transmission line and thicker cables, for no extra useful power at the far end.

**Remedy.** Industrial loads are mostly inductive (motors), so a capacitor bank is connected in parallel to cancel part of the inductive reactance and pull $\cos\phi$ back towards 1.

It is like carrying water in a bucket that sloshes: the sloshing does no good, but you still have to carry it.

questions.q: Show that in a purely capacitive AC circuit the current leads the voltage by $90°$, and write the reactance.
questions.solution:
Let $V = V_{0}\sin\omega t$ across a capacitor $C$.

The charge on it is $q = CV = CV_{0}\sin\omega t$.

The current is the rate at which that charge arrives:

$I = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = \omega CV_{0}\cos\omega t = \omega CV_{0}\sin\left(\omega t + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

So the current reaches its peak a quarter cycle **before** the voltage does — it **leads by $90°$**.

Comparing with $I = I_{0}\sin\left(\omega t + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ gives $I_{0} = \omega CV_{0}$, so

$\mathbf{X_{C} = \dfrac{V_{0}}{I_{0}} = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}}$.

The current is largest when the voltage is changing fastest — that is, as it crosses zero — which is exactly what leading by a quarter cycle means.
